questions.q: How does a window function (e.g. `AVG(price) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`) differ from a `GROUP BY` aggregate?
options: A GROUP BY collapses many rows into one per group; a window function computes a per-row value using nearby rows without collapsing any rows
Window functions can only be used with the AVG function
Window functions require a separate database server, unlike GROUP BY
There is no difference; they always produce identical output
questions.explain: GROUP BY reduces the row count by collapsing groups into aggregates, losing row-level detail. A window function computes an aggregate-like value for each individual row using a defined window of surrounding rows, so every original row survives with an added computed column.

questions.q: In the moving-average example, why is `ma_3` for the very first row (09:30:00) still a real number (190.1) rather than NaN, while `prev_price` for that same row is NaN?
options: This is a bug in DuckDB
ma_3 is computed independently of the ts column
prev_price and ma_3 always return the same value

ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW simply averages whatever rows are available (just the current row, if no prior rows exist yet), while LAG specifically requires a previous row to exist and returns NULL/NaN when there isn't one
questions.explain: The moving-average window clause averages over however many preceding rows actually exist up to CURRENT ROW, so the first row's average is just itself; LAG, by contrast, has no previous row to look at for the first row and correctly returns NaN.

questions.q: What does `ASOF JOIN` do that distinguishes it from a regular equality join?
options: It requires both tables to have the same number of rows
It only joins rows with exactly matching timestamps
For each row on the left, it finds the single best-matching row on the right at or before the left row's timestamp, based on the specified condition
It joins every row on the left to every row on the right (a cross join)
questions.explain: ASOF JOIN is designed specifically for point-in-time matching: given a left-side timestamp, it finds the most recent qualifying right-side row at or before that timestamp, rather than requiring an exact match or producing a full cross product.

questions.q: In the ASOF JOIN example, a request at 09:32:30 matched the price tick at 09:32:00 rather than 09:33:00. Why does that matter for research correctness?
options: The 09:33:00 price was deleted from the table
DuckDB always rounds timestamps down to the nearest minute
It doesn't matter; either match would be equally valid
Matching to 09:33:00 would mean using a price that didn't exist yet at the time of the request -- a lookahead-biased match using future information
questions.explain: Matching a 09:32:30 request to a 09:33:00 price would mean the query 'knew' a price that hadn't occurred yet relative to the request time, which is exactly the lookahead-bias problem flagged in the previous lesson -- ASOF JOIN's at-or-before semantics avoid it by construction.

questions.q: What is the risk of using `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on data that has gaps (e.g. missing trading days)?
options: It operates over whatever rows exist, meaning "the two previous rows" rather than "the two previous calendar days" -- so a gap silently changes what's actually being averaged
ROWS BETWEEN cannot be combined with ORDER BY
The query will fail to execute
DuckDB automatically fills gaps with zero before computing
questions.explain: A ROWS-based window operates over existing rows, not calendar time, so if a day is missing from the data, "2 preceding rows" silently spans a wider calendar gap than intended -- resampling onto a complete time grid (e.g. via generate_series) is the fix when calendar-time semantics are required.
